content: Preterm infants are at an increased risk of developing periventricular haemorrhage (PVH), a condition that can indicate brain damage and potentially lead to neurodevelopmental disorders such as cerebral palsy. It has been hypothesized that administering vitamin K to preterm infants could enhance coagulation and thereby reduce the likelihood of PVH. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of vitamin K given to women at risk of imminent very preterm birth on the prevention of PVH and associated neurological injuries in their infants. The researchers conducted a systematic search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register as of December 20, 2010, to identify relevant studies. The inclusion criteria for the analysis were randomized or quasi-randomized trials in which vitamin K was administered either parenterally or orally to women at risk of imminent preterm delivery. The primary outcomes assessed were neonatal mortality, neonatal neurological morbidity (as determined by the presence of PVH on ultrasound during the first week of life), and long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes. Secondary outcomes included other neonatal morbidities and any adverse effects experienced by the mothers. Two independent reviewers evaluated the eligibility and quality of the trials and extracted the relevant data. A total of eight trials were included in the review, but only seven trials involving 843 women contributed data to the analysis. The quality of the included trials varied. The results showed that antenatal administration of vitamin K was associated with a non-significant reduction in the overall incidence of PVH across all grades (risk ratio [RR] 0.76; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.54 to 1.06). However, there was a statistically significant reduction in the incidence of severe PVH (grades 3 and 4) in infants whose mothers received vitamin K compared to those in the control group (RR 0.58; 95% CI 0.37 to 0.91). When the two quasi-randomized trials were excluded from the analysis, the reduction in all grades of PVH (RR 0.87; 95% CI 0.60 to 1.26) and severe PVH (RR 0.82; 95% CI 0.49 to 1.36) became non-significant. One trial reported a significant reduction in the Bayley Mental Development Index at two years of age for children whose mothers received vitamin K (mean difference [MD] -9.00; 95% CI -16.66 to -1.34). However, this finding was based on a single trial with a high rate of participant loss to follow-up, which limits the reliability of the result. No significant differences were observed in the incidence of other neurodevelopmental abnormalities during pediatric follow-up at 18 to 24 months or at seven years of age between children exposed to antenatal vitamin K and those who were not. In conclusion, the administration of vitamin K to women prior to very preterm birth has not been demonstrated to significantly reduce the risk of PVH in preterm infants or to improve neurodevelopmental outcomes during childhood.
